n0001.title: Replication crisis
n0001.gist: Across many sciences, published findings often fail to reproduce, revealing systemic flaws that researchers are now working to fix.
n0001.question: Replication crisis — why do so many published findings fail to reproduce, and what can be done? (a survey)

n0002.title: Defining replication and its statistics
n0002.gist: Reproducing results is central to science, but definitions of replication vary, and the statistical logic of significance testing underlies most disputes about it.
n0002.question: Replication crisis — what do key terms like replication and statistical significance actually mean? (a conceptual primer)

n0003.title: What replication means
n0003.gist: Reproducing published results is considered essential to science, yet researchers disagree on a single definition, distinguishing direct, systematic and conceptual replication from mere data reanalysis.

n0019.title: Null hypothesis testing basics
n0019.gist: Hypotheses are judged by whether a computed test statistic crosses a threshold, with the p-value showing how surprising the data would be if there were truly no effect.

n0029.title: Errors, power, and p-values
n0029.gist: A test can go wrong in two ways, false positives and false negatives, and the chance of correctly detecting a real effect, called statistical power, governs how trustworthy a result is.

n0039.title: Origins of the crisis
n0039.gist: A cluster of failed replications and exposed bad practices in the early 2010s crystallized decades-old, previously ignored concerns into a named crisis.
n0039.question: Replication crisis — how did a long-standing problem suddenly become a named crisis in the 2010s? (a historical account)

n0040.title: Early 2010s precursor events
n0040.gist: Failed replications of famous social-priming and extrasensory-perception studies, plus shockingly low replication rates in cancer biology, triggered a widely shared sense that research findings could not be trusted as published.

n0048.title: Earlier warnings ignored
n0048.gist: Scholars had flagged weak replication, suspiciously high positive-result rates and low statistical power as far back as the 1960s, but these warnings were repeatedly set aside for decades.

n0054.title: Why it became a crisis now
n0054.gist: Better technology for running and sharing replications, plus a larger and more diverse research community able to scrutinize insiders, turned old complaints into an unavoidable reckoning.

n0056.title: Discipline-specific findings
n0056.gist: Large-scale replication projects across psychology, medicine, economics, nutrition, water science, and AI research consistently found that only a minority of published results reproduce.
n0056.question: Replication crisis — how bad is the replication failure rate, measured field by field? (results from multiple large studies)

n0057.title: Psychology replication projects
n0057.gist: Systematic attempts to redo 100 and then 28 classic psychology studies found roughly a third to half failed to replicate, with successes shrinking in effect size but remaining consistent across different samples.

n0064.title: Medicine and cancer biology
n0064.gist: Landmark medical and cancer studies replicate at strikingly low rates, sometimes just 11%, with effect sizes shrinking by as much as 85% and flawed data found in many clinical trials.

n0073.title: Other fields and AI research
n0073.gist: Economics, water management, and research involving large language models each show their own reproducibility problems, from inflated effect sizes to leaked test data to AI-generated survey contamination.

n0082.title: Surveys on researcher attitudes
n0082.gist: Large surveys of scientists show most have personally failed to reproduce a result, yet still trust published literature, and non-replicable papers are paradoxically cited more often than solid ones.

n0088.title: Causes of the crisis
n0088.gist: The crisis stems from historical publishing pressures, flawed research practices, outright misconduct, weak statistical power, and problems inherent to meta-analysis and hypothesis testing itself.
n0088.question: Replication crisis — what actually causes so many findings to fail replication? (several interacting causes)

n0089.title: Historical and sociological causes
n0089.gist: Science's rapid exponential growth, its commercial commodification, and confusion between its own truth-seeking logic and outside systems like media and profit have eroded quality control.

n0097.title: Publication system problems
n0097.gist: Journals overwhelmingly favor positive, novel results over null findings and replications, so a biased published record likely hides many false positives behind a wall of unreported negative studies.
n0097.sourceHeading: Problems with the publication system in science

n0108.title: Publish-or-perish incentives
n0108.gist: Career pressure to publish frequently pushes researchers toward strategies that make results look publishable rather than valid, since replications bring less recognition than original findings.

n0115.title: Reporting and instrumentation gaps
n0115.gist: Many papers omit the experimental detail needed to redo a study, and ambiguity about whether a null result reflects bad theory or bad instruments lets unreplicable findings accumulate unchecked.

n0123.title: Questionable research practices
n0123.gist: Flexible choices in how data is collected, analyzed, and reported, sometimes amounting to outright fraud, let researchers inflate false-positive rates while technically following the rules.

n0132.title: Low statistical power
n0132.gist: Many fields run studies too small to reliably detect true effects, so even a positive published result has a low chance of being real or of replicating, as shown across psychology, neuroscience, and genetics.

n0141.title: Effect size and meta-analysis issues
n0141.gist: Underpowered studies systematically overestimate effect sizes, and meta-analyses combining them inherit the same biases, with techniques like the fail-safe number only partly correcting for unpublished null results.

n0154.title: P-hacking and flexible analysis
n0154.gist: Trying many statistical tests or stopping data collection early until a significant result appears inflates false-positive rates far above the nominal 5%, a problem that even honest researchers can fall into unknowingly.

n0165.title: Heterogeneity and context sensitivity
n0165.gist: True effects often vary genuinely across studies and settings due to hidden moderators, so even careful, direct replications can reasonably produce very different results without anyone doing anything wrong.

n0176.title: Bayesian view of replication
n0176.gist: Rejecting the null hypothesis at 5% significance does not mean the alternative is 95% likely, because the probability of true replication also depends heavily on a study's prior plausibility and statistical power.

n0184.title: Null hypothesis testing critiqued
n0184.gist: In complex fields like social psychology nearly everything correlates with everything else, so rejecting the null hypothesis offers weak proof of any specific alternative explanation, unlike in simpler experimental sciences.

n0196.title: Public and institutional reactions
n0196.gist: The public remains largely unaware of replication failures, while academics have clashed openly over how harshly to criticize flawed research.
n0196.question: Replication crisis — how have the public and scientific institutions responded to the crisis? (two reactions)

n0197.title: Public awareness and perceptions
n0197.gist: Most of the public has never heard of specific replication failures, and those who have tend to see failed replications as evidence that science's quality control works rather than that it cannot be trusted.

n0202.title: Response in academia
n0202.gist: A prominent psychologist's public defense of flawed research as being unfairly attacked by "methodological terrorists" drew sharp rebuttal from statisticians pointing to her own faulty published work.

n0207.title: Reforming scientific practice
n0207.gist: Researchers are pursuing a broad credibility revolution through pre-registration, transparency, larger samples, and large-scale replication collaborations to rebuild trust in published findings.
n0207.question: Replication crisis — what reforms are being tried to fix science's reliability? (several concrete measures)

n0208.title: Credibility revolution in psychology
n0208.gist: Psychology is embracing a shift toward transparency, preregistration, and stricter evidence standards, treating the replication crisis as an opportunity to rebuild scientific credibility rather than just a scandal.

n0214.title: Reforming scientific publishing
n0214.gist: Metascience, the study of how research itself is done, is driving reforms like clearer methodology reporting, result-blind peer review, and pre-registration to reduce publication bias toward exciting findings.

n0230.title: Tightening statistical standards
n0230.gist: Proposals to lower the significance threshold to p<0.005, track replications with shared databases, and better communicate false-positive risk aim to curb misleading p-value claims, though adoption has lagged.
n0230.sourceHeading: Metadata and digital tools for tracking replications

n0243.title: Larger samples and education
n0243.gist: Because small samples exaggerate effect sizes, reformers push for bigger studies and cross-validation, while also urging that students learn methodology by actually attempting replications themselves.

n0256.title: Tracking and coordinating replications
n0256.gist: New databases track replication attempts to avoid wasted effort, and large international collaborations pool resources to test whether effects generalize across different cultures and labs.

n0267.title: Rethinking scientific method
n0267.gist: Beyond procedural fixes, some scholars argue science needs deeper conceptual change: triangulating evidence, modeling complex interdependence, revising theories, and making all data and code open.
n0267.question: Replication crisis — does fixing science require deeper conceptual change, not just procedural reform? (four proposals)

n0268.title: Triangulation over replication
n0268.gist: Rather than simply repeating one method, researchers argue science should combine multiple independent approaches with different weaknesses, since results that agree across methods are less likely to be mere artifacts.

n0275.title: Complex systems alternative
n0275.gist: The standard linear model assumes mental variables act independently, but treating them instead as interdependent and context-adapting complex systems may better explain why so many psychology replications fail.

n0281.title: Replication as theory revision
n0281.gist: Replication should not just confirm or deny an original finding but actively help build stronger, more generalizable theories, since reproducibility itself best predicts whether a result holds beyond its original context.
n0281.sourceHeading: Replication should seek to revise theories

n0286.title: Open data and software
n0286.gist: Making data, code, and analysis pipelines fully open, as practiced at CERN, is seen as essential for letting others verify results, though the most meticulous open researchers may face disproportionate scrutiny.

n0289.title: See also and references
n0289.gist: A list of related statistical and philosophical concepts and the article's citation sources closes the entry.
